common_name: European False Lily of the Valley (Two-Leaved May Lily)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in fall in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this diminutive Eurasian groundcover spreads by thin rhizomes and is intolerant of summer heat and humidity, so it performs best in cool northern gardens.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, spacing about 8-12 inches apart; European false lily of the valley is a low, spreading woodland groundcover bearing paired, heart-shaped leaves on each short stem and upright racemes of 15-20 tiny, fragrant, four-petaled white star-flowers in late spring, followed by red berries. It is closely related to North America's Maianthemum canadense but has broader, more heart-shaped leaves and a denser flower spike. Plants spread steadily by thick rhizomes into an attractive low mat under deciduous trees, but decline where summers are hot and humid, making them best suited to cool-climate shade gardens. Divide congested colonies in fall to renew vigor and share plants.

common_name: Pacific False Lily of the Valley (Beadruby, Deer Berry)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; this Pacific coastal native spreads aggressively by rhizomes in wet, shaded sites and should be sited with room to colonize or contained where a tidy groundcover is wanted.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing about 10-12 inches apart; Pacific false lily of the valley is a vigorous native groundcover of coastal rainforests from northern California to Alaska, forming dense carpets of heart-shaped, glossy leaves beneath spruce and hemlock canopies. Short spikes of small, four-petaled white flowers appear in late spring, followed by speckled red berries relished by wildlife. It spreads quickly and can be aggressive in the moist, shady conditions it prefers, making it best used as a large-scale woodland groundcover rather than in small refined beds. Very shade tolerant and thrives with regular moisture; it declines in dry soil.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring before shoots emerge, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Siberian Solomon's seal establishes slowly but forms large, long-lived colonies and tolerates root competition and dry shade once mature.

directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing 15-24 inches apart; Siberian Solomon's seal is a tall, robust East Asian woodland perennial whose unbranched, arching to nearly scandent stems carry whorls of narrow, lance-shaped leaves and small clusters of pendant, tubular, greenish-white flowers in the leaf axils in late spring, followed by dark berries in late summer. Reaching 3-5 feet, it is among the largest and most architectural of the cultivated Solomon's seals, valued in traditional Chinese medicine (Huang Jing) as well as ornamentally. It tolerates a wide range of shaded conditions, including competition from tree roots, and spreads gradually by thick rhizomes to form substantial colonies over time.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; green fairy bells spreads quickly by rhizomes to form a large colony, so give it room away from smaller, less vigorous companions.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12-18 inches apart; green fairy bells is an easy-to-grow woodland perennial native to Japan, Korea, and northeastern China, forming winter-dormant clumps of upright, leafy stalks that carry nodding, pale greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers in spring followed by small black berries in fall. It spreads more readily than the related Disporum sessile, colonizing shaded ground via underground rhizomes to create an attractive, low-maintenance groundcover. Site it away from choice, slow-growing neighbors that could be overrun, and pair with hostas, ferns, and other vigorous shade perennials.

common_name: Samurai Toad Lily (Gold-Edged Variegated Toad Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Samurai' is grown chiefly for its creamy-gold leaf margins, which color best with some morning sun or bright filtered light.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, spacing 15-18 inches apart; 'Samurai' is a compact sport of the Formosa toad lily selected for its shiny, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves edged in creamy gold, providing season-long foliage interest well before the late-summer flowers appear. In late summer to early fall, clusters of small, purple, heavily freckled, orchid-like flowers open in the upper leaf axils and stem tips, echoing the species but on a shorter, more garden-friendly plant. Give it a touch more light than deep-shade toad lilies to keep the variegation crisp, but protect it from hot afternoon sun. Divide congested clumps in early spring to maintain vigor and increase plantings.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plants Database

common_name: Vic Pawlowski's Gold Lily of the Valley (Gold-Striped Foliage Convallaria)

planting.note: Plant pips (rhizome divisions) in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; a little early morning or late afternoon sun helps keep the gold leaf striping strong on 'Vic Pawlowski's Gold', which is more stable than many other variegated lily of the valley selections.

directions: Plant pips shallowly in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, spacing 6-9 inches apart; 'Vic Pawlowski's Gold' bears the classic sweetly fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers of lily of the valley in late spring above broad leaves boldly striped along their length in bright golden-yellow. Unlike some variegated Convallaria selections that revert quickly to plain green, this cultivar holds its gold striping well, especially with some direct morning or late-day sun to reinforce the pigment. It spreads by rhizomes to form a colorful, slow-to-moderate groundcover colony and goes fully dormant in summer. All parts are toxic if ingested.
